title: Are We the Loud Minority - The Truth About Physical Media

segments.text: I want to have an honest conversation
and this one might sting a little for
people like me who love physical [music]
media. We talk a lot about the
importance of owning your games, owning
your comics, having something tangible
on a shelf that can't be taken away from
you with a server shutdown or licensing
change. And I agree with all of that.
I'm pro- physical media as you all know.
And as a business owner here at the
Ripoververse, we built our entire model
around physical products. That's our
priority. But I [music] think we need to
ask ourselves an uncomfortable question
when we say physical media matters. Is
the market actually agreeing with us or
are we the loud minority? Let's look at
the numbers. In gaming, roughly 90% of
all game sales are now digital. On PC,
it's not even a conversation. Steam has
147 million monthly active users and
control 75% of the PC digital
distribution market. Physical PC games
essentially are extinct. We're talking
about 99% digital on that platform. On
console, it's heading in the same
direction. PS5 software is about 78%
digital. Xbox is at 91%. The only
platform still holding the line is
Nintendo, where physical media and
digital are closer to a 50/50 split. And
even that number is creeping toward
digital every single year. Physical game
spending in the US is down over 85% from
its 2008 peak. Best Buy, you know,
stopped selling physical movies
entirely. Retailers, they're shrinking
the shelf space and the infrastructure
that supported physical media is
disappearing in real time. Now, here's
where it gets a little interesting.
Comics tell a slightly different story.
In US, physical comics still account for
almost like 90% of the revenue.
Globally, though, it's closer to about
60 to 70%. the collector culture, the
comic shop ecosystem and the convention
circuit, all of that keeps physical
comics alive in a way that gaming just
they clearly moved past. But even comics
digital is growing at nearly double the
rate of physical. The trajectory is
clear even if the timeline is a little
longer. So what do we make of this? I
think there are two realities existing
at the same time right now. The first
reality is that physical media
objectively matters. Ownership matters.
We've already seen what happens when
digital storefronts pull [music]
content. Games disappear, libraries
shrink, and you paid for a license, not
a product. That's a real concern, and
it's not like a hypothetical anymore.
It's happening. But the second reality
is that the overwhelming majority of
consumers have made their choice and
they chose convenience. They chose like
clicking a button and having one game
ready in minutes over driving to a
store. They chose not caring about Shelf
because their library lives in the
cloud. So far, the market has spoken and
unfortunately it hasn't sided with us.
Now, I'm not saying we're wrong. As I
said, the Riververse here, we lead with
physical media and we always will. We
just launched [music] digital as an
option because the demand was there and
we wanted to fill things out, but
physical is going to always be our
backbone. I believe in that model, but I
also believe in being honest. And
honestly, when we look at the numbers,
the people who care deeply about
physical media are passionate, but we
are outnumbered. The question isn't
whether physical media is better. The
question is whether enough people care
to have it survive long term. And right
now the answer from the market is not
